claim: Improving in one aspect of a task can undermine performance in another in single cells.
source: Improving in one aspect of a task can undermine performance in another, but how such opposing demands play out in single cells and impact on fitness is mostly unknown.
evidence: This is a general statement introducing the research problem, supported by the subsequent experimental findings in the manuscript.

claim: The HOG signaling network in budding yeast increases cellular survival by assigning high response speed and high response accuracy to two separate input pathways.
source: Here we study budding yeast in dynamic environments of hyperosmotic stress and show how the corresponding signalling network increases cellular survival both by assigning the requirements of high response speed and high response accuracy to two separate input pathways and by having these pathways interact to converge on Hog1, a p38 MAP kinase.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript showing differential performance of mutants with single pathways.

claim: Cells with only the Sln1 pathway (fast mutant) are fitter in sudden stress.
source: Cells with only the less accurate, reflex-like pathway are fitter in sudden stress, whereas cells with only the slow, more accurate pathway are fitter in increasing but fluctuating stress.
evidence: This is supported by fitness measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Cells with only the Sho1 pathway (slow mutant) are fitter in increasing but fluctuating stress.
source: Cells with only the less accurate, reflex-like pathway are fitter in sudden stress, whereas cells with only the slow, more accurate pathway are fitter in increasing but fluctuating stress.
evidence: This is supported by fitness measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Fast responses have lower accuracy in engineering systems.
source: In engineering, for example, it is well-known that fast responses have lower accuracy and that higher amplifications can cause overshooting and unintended oscillations (Astrom and Murray, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to engineering literature.

claim: Signal transduction has evolved to reduce trade-offs because performance in both speed and accuracy are likely under selection.
source: At the cellular level, we expect signal transduction has evolved to reduce such trade-offs because performance in, for example, both speed and accuracy are likely to be under selection (Shoval et al., 2012; Lan et al., 2012; Siggia and Vergassola, 2013).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Yeast cells can shrink in seconds following an abrupt increase in environmental osmolarity.
source: Following an abrupt increase in environmental osmolarity, yeast cells can shrink in seconds (Hohmann, 2002) and must therefore respond quickly.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The osmotic stress response in yeast is metabolically costly, involving the synthesis of glycerol.
source: Their response though is metabolically costly, involving the synthesis of the osmoprotectant glycerol, and inaccurate hyperactivation of the signalling network can be highly deleterious (Tao et al., 1999; Mitchell et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The HOG network has a Y-shaped structure with two input pathways converging on Pbs2.
source: The Hyper-Osmolarity-Glycerol (HOG) network has a Y-shaped structure with two input pathways both converging on Pbs2, a MAP kinase kinase (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the schematic in Figure 1A and citations to prior work.

claim: The Sln1 pathway uses a two-component phosphorelay analogous to those in bacteria.
source: One branch of the Y, the Sln1 pathway, uses a two-component phosphorelay, analogous to those in bacteria, to propagate the signal (Posas et al., 1996; Posas and Saito, 1998)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The Sho1 pathway uses protein kinases similar to signalling in higher organisms.
source: the other, the Sho1 branch, uses protein kinases, similar to signalling in higher organisms (Posas and Saito, 1997; Tatebayashi et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Pbs2 activates Hog1 via phosphorylation.
source: Once activated, Pbs2 in turn activates Hog1 via phosphorylation (Brewster et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Hog1 can translocate into the nucleus upon activation.
source: Similarly to MAP kinases in mammalian cells, Hog1 can then translocate into the nucleus.
evidence: This is supported by knowledge of MAP kinase behavior and observed in the experimental data.

claim: Hog1 increases intracellular glycerol concentration through cytosolic changes and altering gene expression.
source: Upon activation, Hog1 causes an increase in the intracellular concentration of glycerol, yeast's main osmoprotectant, in two ways (Saito and Posas, 2012): first, through cytosolic changes, such as diverting glycolysis towards synthesizing glycerol and closing channels that export glycerol, and, second, through altering gene expression to increase the numbers of enzymes involved in glycerol synthesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The Sln1 branch is faster than the Sho1 branch.
source: The two branches of the Y may sense stress differently (Reiser et al., 2003; Tanaka et al., 2014) and are known to operate at different time-scales (Maeda et al., 1995; Hersen et al., 2008): the Sln1 branch being faster than the Sho1 branch.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: There is no reported phenotype for strains having only the Sln1 branch.
source: Mutants that have only one branch of the Y have been created (Maeda et al., 1995; Reiser et al., 2003; Hersen et al., 2008; Macia et al., 2009; Schaber et al., 2012; English et al., 2015), but there is no reported phenotype for strains having only the Sln1 branch, and the Sho1 pathway is often considered redundant (Klipp et al., 2005; Muzzey et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The Sho1 pathway is often considered redundant.
source: Mutants that have only one branch of the Y have been created (Maeda et al., 1995; Reiser et al., 2003; Hersen et al., 2008; Macia et al., 2009; Schaber et al., 2012; English et al., 2015), but there is no reported phenotype for strains having only the Sln1 branch, and the Sho1 pathway is often considered redundant (Klipp et al., 2005; Muzzey et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The nuclear level of Hog1 has long been used as a read-out of the HOG network's response.
source: The nuclear level of Hog1 has long been used as a read-out of the HOG network's response (Mettetal et al., 2008; Muzzey et al., 2009; Pelet et al., 2011; Babazadeh et al., 2013; Mitchell et al., 2015) and is strongly correlated with Hog1 phosphorylation (Reiser et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Nuclear Hog1 is strongly correlated with Hog1 phosphorylation.
source: The nuclear level of Hog1 has long been used as a read-out of the HOG network's response (Mettetal et al., 2008; Muzzey et al., 2009; Pelet et al., 2011; Babazadeh et al., 2013; Mitchell et al., 2015) and is strongly correlated with Hog1 phosphorylation (Reiser et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: When exposed to hyperosmotic stress, cellular volume shrinks, Hog1 undergoes nuclear translocation, and cells arrest.
source: When exposed to hyperosmotic stress, cellular volume shrinks, Hog1 undergoes nuclear translocation, and cells arrest. Growth typically resumes once the volume has recovered.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and supported by experimental observations.

claim: A reduction in volume causes Hog1 to translocate within minutes.
source: A reduction in volume causes Hog1 to translocate within minutes and the recovery of the volume correlates with levels of nuclear Hog1.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D,E with population and single-cell data.

claim: The recovery of cellular volume correlates with levels of nuclear Hog1.
source: A reduction in volume causes Hog1 to translocate within minutes and the recovery of the volume correlates with levels of nuclear Hog1.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D,E with population and single-cell data.

claim: In steps of hyperosmotic stress, the mean response of Hog1 in the fast mutants is equivalent to wild-type cells.
source: Indeed, in steps, the mean response of Hog1 in the fast mutants is equivalent to wild-type cells, but the slow mutant has typically longer response times and a lower maximum level of nuclear localization (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A with experimental data.

claim: The slow mutant has typically longer response times and a lower maximum level of nuclear localization in steps of stress.
source: Indeed, in steps, the mean response of Hog1 in the fast mutants is equivalent to wild-type cells, but the slow mutant has typically longer response times and a lower maximum level of nuclear localization (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A with experimental data.

claim: The wild-type and fast mutant have almost identical mean volume responses in steps of stress.
source: Considering the reduction in cellular volume, the wild-type and fast response are again almost identical on average, and the longer response time of the slow mutant is reflected in a slower volume recovery (Figure 2A), particularly in larger steps (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 with experimental data.

claim: The slow mutant has a slower volume recovery, particularly in larger steps.
source: Considering the reduction in cellular volume, the wild-type and fast response are again almost identical on average, and the longer response time of the slow mutant is reflected in a slower volume recovery (Figure 2A), particularly in larger steps (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 with experimental data.

claim: In all strains, the mean volume and the mean level of nuclear Hog1 simultaneously go to zero.
source: In all strains, the mean volume and the mean level of nuclear Hog1 simultaneously go to zero (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A with experimental data.

claim: The accuracy of the fast mutant remains consistently lower than the wild-type.
source: Although the accuracy of all strains increases as the volume recovers, it is the wild-type and the slow mutant that behave similarly, and the correlation for the fast mutant remains consistently lower than the wild-type.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C with correlation data from single cells.

claim: The wild-type and slow mutant have similar accuracy in matching Hog1 adaptation to volume recovery.
source: Although the accuracy of all strains increases as the volume recovers, it is the wild-type and the slow mutant that behave similarly, and the correlation for the fast mutant remains consistently lower than the wild-type.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C with correlation data from single cells.

claim: The Hog1 behaviour in the fast mutant during adaptation is more noisy than the wild-type.
source: This discrepancy between the mean (Figure 2A) and the single-cell results (Figure 2C) implies that the Hog1 behaviour in the fast mutant during adaptation is more noisy than the wild-type.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of mean and single-cell data.

claim: As Hog1 adapts, Hog1 in the fast mutant becomes less informative on the level of stress.
source: As Hog1 adapts, Hog1 in the fast mutant becomes less informative on the level of stress and its distribution of adaptation times is broader than the wild-type for some stresses.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D with mutual information analysis.

claim: The slow pathway is more sensitive to the system's integral feedback than the fast pathway.
source: We reasoned that if the slow mutant is able to gradually increase its accuracy (Figure 2C) then the slow pathway should be more sensitive to the integral feedback. Indeed, the slow pathway unlike the fast pathway is known to have multiple types of osmo-sensors (Tanaka et al., 2014) and so may better sense the increase in volume resulting from the increase in glycerol.
evidence: This is supported by experimental perturbation data in Figure 3 and citations.

claim: The slow pathway has multiple types of osmo-sensors.
source: Indeed, the slow pathway unlike the fast pathway is known to have multiple types of osmo-sensors (Tanaka et al., 2014) and so may better sense the increase in volume resulting from the increase in glycerol.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Decreasing expression of PBS2 reduces the maximum level of Hog1 localization but increases its adaptation time in both the wild-type and slow mutant.
source: Decreasing expression of PBS2 reduces the maximum level of Hog1 localization but increases its adaptation time in both the wild-type and slow mutant (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and C with experimental data.

claim: For the fast pathway, there is little increase in the adaptation time when PBS2 is decreased.
source: In contrast, for the fast pathway, there is little increase in the adaptation time (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D with experimental data.

claim: The ratio of adaptation time of Hog1 to the adaptation time of the volume decreases significantly only for the fast mutant when PBS2 is reduced.
source: Both the ratio of adaptation time of Hog1 to the adaptation time of the volume and the accuracy decreases significantly only for the fast mutant (Figure 3D inset with p<10−6 using a two-sided Wilcoxon rank sum test for equal medians calculated by pooling distributions from single cells).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D inset with statistical analysis.

claim: The fast pathway has the potential to respond to the time-derivative of its input.
source: The insensitivity of the adaptation time of Hog1 and the sensitivity of the adaptation time of the volume for the fast mutant in these experiments (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1) suggest the existence of a mechanism within the fast pathway that decreases signalling of Hog1 before the volume completely recovers. This additional adaptation within the pathway to a step of stress implies that the fast pathway has the potential to respond to the time-derivative of its input (Block et al., 1983; Behar et al., 2007; Alon, 2007).
evidence: This is inferred from experimental observations and supported by citations.

claim: The fast mutant responds quicker than the wild-type in ramp inputs.
source: We observe a systematic increase in the amplitude of Hog1 in the fast mutant over that of the wild-type and the mutant responds quicker (Figure 4A and B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and B with experimental data.

claim: The mean wild-type response is closer in amplitude to the slow mutant during adaptation in ramps.
source: Indeed, the mean wild-type response is closer in amplitude to the slow mutant, particularly during adaptation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A with experimental data.

claim: The overshoot of the fast mutant is consistent with stronger derivative action in the fast pathway.
source: The overshoot of the fast mutant (Figure 4C) is consistent with stronger derivative action in the fast pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data in Figure 4C.

claim: The wild-type response is generated by interactions between the two pathways and is not an average of their responses.
source: We note that the wild-type response is generated by interactions between the two pathways and is not an average of their responses (Figure 4A): the maximum amplitude of the wild-type strain increases linearly with the gradient of the ramp although the response of strains with each individual pathway does not (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and C with experimental data.

claim: Both the fast mutant and the wild-type have the highest statistical dependency with the smoothed time-derivative of the input in fluctuating ramps.
source: As expected, both the fast mutant and the wild-type have the highest statistical dependency with the (smoothed) time-derivative (Figure 4E and F; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E and F with cross-correlation and mutual information analysis.

claim: The slow pathway provides accuracy at the expense of speed.
source: Together our results indicate contrasting roles for the two input pathways: the slow pathway provides accuracy at the expense of speed (Figure 3); the fast pathway provides speed at the expense of accuracy (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The fast pathway provides speed at the expense of accuracy.
source: Together our results indicate contrasting roles for the two input pathways: the slow pathway provides accuracy at the expense of speed (Figure 3); the fast pathway provides speed at the expense of accuracy (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The outputs of the two pathways do not always sum to give the wild-type response.
source: Further, the response to ramps of stress implies the outputs of the two pathways do not always sum to give the wild-type response (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A with experimental data.

claim: The model captures the differences between the mutants and the wild-type in both steps and ramps.
source: The model captures the differences between the mutants and the wild-type we observe in both steps (Figure 5B) and ramps (Figure 5C) and provides insight into how two opposing tasks can be implemented in the network by having specialized subnetworks.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B and C with model predictions.

claim: Derivative action is a way to increase gain while maintaining structural stability.
source: Derivative action is a well-known way to increase gain while maintaining structural stability (Astrom and Murray, 2008), and derivative action in the fast pathway enables that pathway's high gain.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to engineering literature.

claim: The derivative action in the fast pathway is open loop, responding to the input not the error.
source: The derivative action is open loop, responding to the input not the error, and therefore reduces the coupling of the fast pathway to the integral feedback, undermining the network's accuracy.
evidence: This is inferred from the model structure and experimental observations.

claim: The slow pathway has a lower gain and is therefore slower but more stable.
source: The slow pathway has a lower gain and is therefore slower but more stable (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3B and C.

claim: The fast mutant outperforms the slow mutant in steps of stress.
source: Quantifying the number of unfit cells, we find that the selective advantage of having both input pathways is revealed by exposing cells to environments with a range of different dynamics: the fast mutant outperforms the slow mutant in steps of stress and the slow mutant outperforms the fast mutant in ramps of fluctuating stress (Figure 6A; Videos 2 and 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A with fitness measurements.

claim: The slow mutant outperforms the fast mutant in ramps of fluctuating stress.
source: Quantifying the number of unfit cells, we find that the selective advantage of having both input pathways is revealed by exposing cells to environments with a range of different dynamics: the fast mutant outperforms the slow mutant in steps of stress and the slow mutant outperforms the fast mutant in ramps of fluctuating stress (Figure 6A; Videos 2 and 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A with fitness measurements.

claim: The wild-type performs both speed and accuracy tasks and always has the highest probability of survival.
source: With its two input pathways, the wild-type performs both tasks and is both fast and accurate, always having the highest probability of survival.
evidence: This is supported by fitness data in Figure 6A.

claim: Trade-offs in performance can undermine signalling in a single input pathway.
source: We have thus shown that trade-offs in performance can undermine signalling in a single input pathway with either speed being sacrificed for accuracy or vice versa, but that by having two input pathways, each specializing to particular task, signalling networks can mitigate these trade-offs (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by all experimental data.

claim: By having two input pathways, each specializing to a particular task, signalling networks can mitigate trade-offs.
source: We have thus shown that trade-offs in performance can undermine signalling in a single input pathway with either speed being sacrificed for accuracy or vice versa, but that by having two input pathways, each specializing to particular task, signalling networks can mitigate these trade-offs (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by all experimental data.

claim: The Sln1 pathway is a fast reflex-like response that provides speed necessary to survive sudden shocks but at the expense of accuracy.
source: In the HOG network, the Sln1 pathway is a fast reflex-like response that provides the speed necessary to survive sudden shocks but at the expense of accuracy, and alone can cause adaptation of Hog1 before recovery of the cellular volume.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The Sln1 pathway alone can cause adaptation of Hog1 before recovery of the cellular volume.
source: In the HOG network, the Sln1 pathway is a fast reflex-like response that provides the speed necessary to survive sudden shocks but at the expense of accuracy, and alone can cause adaptation of Hog1 before recovery of the cellular volume.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: Fast mutants have a shorter duration of Hog1 phosphorylation compared to wild-type cells.
source: Consistent with this observation, Macia et al. report that fast mutants have a shorter duration of Hog1 phosphorylation compared to wild-type cells (Macia et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The Sho1 pathway provides accuracy at the expense of speed by specializing to sensing the integral feedback.
source: In contrast, the Sho1 pathway provides accuracy at the expense of speed and by specializing to sensing the integral feedback coming from volume recovery is more sensitive to the cell's internal state and the history of the extracellular stress.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The Sho1 pathway is more sensitive to the cell's internal state and the history of the extracellular stress.
source: In contrast, the Sho1 pathway provides accuracy at the expense of speed and by specializing to sensing the integral feedback coming from volume recovery is more sensitive to the cell's internal state and the history of the extracellular stress.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The Sho1 branch primarily monitors osmotic changes during normal growth.
source: This behaviour is consistent with earlier speculations that the Sho1 branch primarily monitors osmotic changes during normal growth (Hohmann, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The Sho1 pathway interacts with the actin cytoskeleton.
source: If the integral feedback is to allow recovery of the volume, the network must remember the cellular volume before the stress (Astrom and Murray, 2008), and the Sho1 pathway interacts with the actin cytoskeleton (Tanaka et al., 2014), which might allow information from cell morphology and growth to be integrated with activation of Hog1.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The two input pathways have been reported to have different thresholds of activation.
source: The two input pathways have been reported to have different thresholds of activation (Macia et al., 2009), but our data and modelling points towards a re-interpretation in terms of different gains for the pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Only the wild-type response increases linearly with the gradient of a ramp of stress.
source: Our data points towards it being the interaction between the two pathways that increases the dynamic range: we observe that only the wild-type response increases linearly with the gradient of a ramp of stress (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C with experimental data.

claim: A single fast input pathway controlling the integral feedback would have structural instabilities in its dynamics because of the high gain necessary for high speed.
source: A potentially alternative architecture of the HOG signalling network is to have a single fast input pathway controlling the integral feedback. Such a network, however, would not only have structural instabilities in its dynamics because of the high gain necessary for high speed, but also would be more likely to become insensitive to the cell's internal state for sufficiently high stress.
evidence: This is a theoretical argument based on control theory principles.

claim: In large stress, all Hog1 molecules can become activated and the output of the HOG controller is then saturated.
source: In large stress, all Hog1 molecules can become activated and the output of the HOG controller is then saturated. This saturation will happen for shocks of smaller magnitude for systems with high gain and causes a loss of accuracy because the system is then in open loop and is unable to exploit the integral feedback.
evidence: This is a theoretical argument based on control theory principles.

claim: Having a slow pathway that inhibits the fast pathway helps prevent saturation of Hog1 activity.
source: Having a slow pathway that inhibits the fast pathway helps prevent saturation of Hog1 activity and so increases sensitivity to the integral feedback for higher levels of stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the model and experimental observations.

claim: Competing for Pbs2 is one possible means of cross-inhibition between the pathways.
source: Competing for Pbs2 is one possible means of cross-inhibition between the pathways, but multiple feedbacks, both positive and negative, exist within the HOG network (Hao et al., 2007; Macia et al., 2009; Sharifian et al., 2015; English et al., 2015), and a feedback-based interaction is possible.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Multiple feedbacks, both positive and negative, exist within the HOG network.
source: Competing for Pbs2 is one possible means of cross-inhibition between the pathways, but multiple feedbacks, both positive and negative, exist within the HOG network (Hao et al., 2007; Macia et al., 2009; Sharifian et al., 2015; English et al., 2015), and a feedback-based interaction is possible.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Biochemistry can be used to measure a time-derivative on time-scales as fast as seconds.
source: That biochemistry can be used to measure a time-derivative on a time-scales as fast as seconds is well established (Block et al., 1983), and, in analogy with bacterial chemotaxis, we expect that upstream signalling in the fast pathway encodes a short-term memory of the level of the input to allow comparison of the current level to a value in the past.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Using inputs with varying dynamics is important to uncover the logic behind cellular signalling.
source: More generally, our results confirm the importance of using inputs with varying dynamics to uncover the logic behind cellular signalling (Nurse, 2008; Alexander et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental results and citations.

claim: In the wild, organisms are exposed to signals with a wider range of temporal behaviours than the constant inputs typically studied in the laboratory.
source: In the wild, organisms are exposed to signals with a wider range of temporal behaviours then the constant inputs typically studied in the laboratory (López-Maury et al., 2008), and signal transduction is likely to have evolved to allow organisms to differentiate between such signals or at least between classes of signals (Bowsher and Swain, 2014; Tkačik and Bialek, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Signal transduction is likely to have evolved to allow organisms to differentiate between different classes of signals.
source: In the wild, organisms are exposed to signals with a wider range of temporal behaviours then the constant inputs typically studied in the laboratory (López-Maury et al., 2008), and signal transduction is likely to have evolved to allow organisms to differentiate between such signals or at least between classes of signals (Bowsher and Swain, 2014; Tkačik and Bialek, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Dynamic inputs have been successfully used to understand signalling responses in bacteria, yeast, and mammalian cells.
source: Although such work is still in its infancy, dynamic inputs have been successfully used to understand signalling responses in, for example, bacteria (Young et al., 2013), yeast (Hao et al., 2013), and mammalian cells (Kellogg and Tay, 2015), and, with the ease of use of microfluidics (Bennett and Hasty, 2009), we believe should become commonplace.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cellular signalling is vulnerable to fundamental trade-offs in performance.
source: In conclusion, we have shown that cellular signalling is vulnerable to fundamental trade-offs in performance, but that these vulnerabilities can be overcome by distributing tasks to different parts of the network and integrating together the outputs of this division of labour.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by all experimental data.

claim: Trade-off vulnerabilities can be overcome by distributing tasks to different parts of the network and integrating together the outputs.
source: In conclusion, we have shown that cellular signalling is vulnerable to fundamental trade-offs in performance, but that these vulnerabilities can be overcome by distributing tasks to different parts of the network and integrating together the outputs of this division of labour.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by all experimental data.

claim: Improvements in performance by the specialization of subnetworks to different tasks exist broadly within cellular signal transduction.
source: We therefore expect such improvements in performance by the specialization of subnetworks to different tasks to exist broadly within cellular signal transduction.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings of the study.

claim: All strains used were constructed using PCR-based genomic integration and validated by colony PCR.
source: All strains (Table 1) were constructed using PCR-based genomic integration and were validated by colony PCR.
evidence: This describes the methods used to construct the strains.

claim: The Tet-off system was used for inducible expression of PBS2.
source: For inducible expression of PBS2, we used the Tet-off system (Bellí et al., 1998), for which doxycycline causes repression.
evidence: This describes the methods used for gene expression control.

claim: The mutants showed equivalent growth from wild-type strains in XY media with 2% glucose over 24 hr.
source: The mutants showed equivalent growth from wild-type strains in XY media with 2% glucose over 24 hr (data not shown).
evidence: This is an experimental observation about strain growth.

claim: Cells were grown at 30°C overnight in 2% glucose in synthetic complete media.
source: Cells were grown at 30°C overnight in 2% glucose in synthetic complete (SC) media, diluted by a factor of 1/20 into fresh SC with 2% glucose next morning and incubated for 4 hr at 30°C.
evidence: This describes the cell culture methods.

claim: The ALCATRAS microfluidic device was used to trap and expose cells to osmotic stress.
source: Cells were then loaded into the ALCATRAS chamber (Crane et al., 2014), which was already filled with SC with 2% glucose and 0.05% bovine serum albumin (BSA) to facilitate cell loading and reduce the formation of clumps of cells.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: Two syringe pumps were used to create dynamic environmental conditions.
source: Two syringe pumps (Aladdin NE-1002X) were used to create dynamic environmental conditions. The first pump was loaded with SC and 2% glucose; the second pump was loaded with SC with 2% glucose and sorbitol.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: The dye Cy5 was added to the syringe containing sorbitol and used to monitor the sorbitol dynamics.
source: The dye Cy5 was added to the syringe containing sorbitol and used to monitor the sorbitol dynamics. The concentration of sorbitol we report corresponds to the level of fluorescence from Cy5.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: A multi-chamber version of ALCATRAS was developed to expose multiple strains to the same environmental conditions.
source: To expose multiple strains to the same environmental conditions and to optimize data acquisition, we developed a multi-chamber version of ALCATRAS, which allows different strains to be loaded into distinct chambers but still be exposed to the same extracellular media.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: The volume of each cell was approximated from the total area of the cell in the fluorescence image.
source: The volume of each cell was approximated from the total area of the cell in the fluorescence image (Gordon et al., 2007; Muzzey et al., 2009). We calculated the radius of the circle that has the same area as the cross-sectional area of the cell and used this radius to compute the volume assuming spherical cells.
evidence: This describes the data analysis methods.

claim: Nuclear accumulation of Hog1 was quantified by calculating the ratio between the average of the five brightest pixels within the cell and the median fluorescence of the whole cell.
source: We quantified the nuclear accumulation of Hog1 by calculating the ratio between the average of the five brightest pixels within the cell and the median fluorescence of the whole cell. This measure is robust to bleaching of the fluorophore and has been widely used (Cai et al., 2008; Hao and O'Shea, 2011; Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the data analysis methods.
